html:
On 12 March 1171 the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos had all Venetians in his empire arrested and their ships and goods seized. Thousands were jailed in Constantinople alone. The move led to a short war with Venice.

Since the Golden Bull of 1082, Venetian merchants had traded tax-free in the empire and grown rich and unpopular. Manuel was also drawing closer to Venice's rivals, Genoa and Pisa. When the Genoese quarter at Galata was attacked, he blamed the Venetians and struck.

Doge Vitale II Michiel led a fleet to the Aegean in 1171. Manuel kept him talking while plague broke out among the crews wintering on Chios. The fleet came home sick and beaten, and the doge was killed by an angry crowd in Venice in 1172. Relations were only partly repaired, and Venetians did not forget. Among the envoys sent to Constantinople in these years was Enrico Dandolo, who would lead Venice in the sack of the city in 1204.
sum: On 12 March 1171 the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos had all Venetians in his empire arrested and their ships and goods seized. Thousands were jailed in Constantinople alone. The move led to a short war with Venice.
